newsitem.title: UK: Sterling edgy ahead of by-election result.
newsitem.headline: Sterling edgy ahead of by-election result.

text.p: Sterling was choppy in Europe, flirting with 2.75 marks, as the market awaited the result of a key British Parliamentary by-election which threatens to push the Conservatives into a minority government.
Traders said while the currency market has already factored-in a Labour win at Wirral, a prosperous corner of England and once safe Tory seat, the margin of a Labour victory is the key.
"Wirral could have potential pitfalls for the government in the sense that it could argue for a general election sooner rather than later," said David Brown, chief economist at Bear Stearns.

Other economists have said that a landslide win could also give Labour, out of government since 1979, a mandate to be tougher on economic policy and some have even raised the possibility of it reneging on its pre-election commitments.
"The South Wirral by-election should be seen as an indicator of voting intentions for the forthcoming UK general election," said Joe Prendergast, foreign exchange strategist at Merrill Lynch.
Prendergast said while a Labour victory at Wirral is widely discounted, the margin of victory may be of great importance to sterling.

"If a Labour victory in South Wirral were to be with a majority of much less than 5,000 votes, there should be concern that the general election outcome may be closer than most recent opinion polls predict," said Prendergast.
That scenario, say analysts, would threaten a hung Parliament at the general election - which must be called by May - and pose a worse scenario for the currency.
Around midday sterling stood at 2.7495/05 marks, just down from 2.7560/70 in late Europe on Wednesday and below key psychological resistance at 2.7500 marks.
Against the dollar, sterling was trading at $1.6280/90 compared to $1.6321/31 in late Europe.
The fact that the pound was not firmer on Thursday, in tandem with a recovering dollar, was also reflecting the jitters ahead of the by-election results.
"There is a bit of nervousness ahead of the Wirral-election (result)," said a senior trader at a UK bank.

Any set-back for sterling, however, is likely to be shor-tlived though because markets now see little difference between Labour's - once the high spending, high taxing party - and the Conservatives' macro-economic policies.
Both domestic and foreign investors are fairly comfortable with the prospect of the next government being a Labour one, said Brown.
